newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: French bond futures settled lower on Thursday amid concern about ongoing tension in the runup to European monetary union and weakness in the U.S. and German bond markets, analysts said.

French bond futures started to decline during Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's policy speech to parliament and while some traders put the weakness down to fact he had pledged to fulfill his campaign promises, others said stronger-than-expected U.S. economic data had unsettled bond markets.
The September bond future slipped from a high of 129.06 at the start of the speech to settle at 128.66, down 0.22.
Some traders in Paris said French bonds followed Bunds down after a sharp rise in the Philadelphia Fed's June business activity index had revived fears of U.S. interest rate rises.

Others said concerns Jospin's commitment to honouring his campaign pledges, which risk pushing the 1997 budget deficit well above the strict three percent Maastricht target and increasing tension with Germany, had dragged both markets lower.

One analyst said the fact there were so many conflicting explanations for the decline showed core European bond markets had become too optimistic about monetary union after the Amsterdam summit and traders were looking for excuses to sell.

"Jospin was expected to come out along the lines of not quite fulfilling all their campaign pledges but he said he will and this was combined with the weak U.S. market," he said. "People were feeling secure the U.S. wouldn't do anything, now they're saying the second quarter and the third quarter won't be so weak and the whole thing has been turned on its head."
"The big picture is that there's a lot of disagreement (in Europe) and what they did in Amsterdam is paper over the cracks and the cracks are going to reappear very quickly," he said.
Economists said it was positive Jospin only increased the minimum wage by four percent but much uncertainty remained.

The new prime minister warned that the state of public finances looked "serious" but it was unclear what this would mean for the French public deficit in 1997 until a mini-budget was unveiled after the summer.

"Tension and pressure are going to maintained all through the summmer," Philippe Brossard, head of research at ABN Amro Finance said. "There's still a much higher probability that (EMU) will happen than not, but odds are not increasing. The Germans are not happy and there's always worry, for one pretext or another, they will ask to postpone."
He said the Jospin speech contained several new spending commitments and that he expected the 1997 public deficit to come in, eventually at about 3.3 percent of gross domestic product.

Several analysts said end investors were not strong buyers of French bonds and this meant the market was especially vulnerable to worries either about European countries' fiscal problems or selloffs in the United States.
"We've not seen many final investors, they look very reluctant to invest these days so when you have a selloff in the U.S. market it turns into a larger selloff in Europe," one said.

The French September bond contract extended its losses in electronic GLOBEX trading and was testing strong support at 128.48/50. September PIBOR, however, was unchanged from the end of pit-trading at 96.52.
The spread between French and German 10-year bond yields narrowed slightly to minus 10 basis points during the Jospin speech but was unchanged at minus 12 late in the session.
The French franc slipped slightly against the mark and was trading at 3.3754 late on Thursday compared with 3.3735 on Wednesday.
